claim: Across 8 NAS methods (DARTS, StacNAS, PDARTS, MANAS, CNAS, NSGANET, ENAS, NAO) on 5 datasets, most methods achieve only a small relative improvement (RI) over the average randomly sampled architecture from the same search space, and several are RI-negative on individual datasets.
stance_target: search algorithms in constrained CNN search spaces struggle to reliably beat random sampling
scope_conditions: 8 NAS methods, 5 image classification datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, SPORT8, MIT67, FLOWERS102), search time <4 GPU-days
quoted_support: Surprisingly, we find that many NAS techniques struggle to significantly beat the average architecture baseline.
numbers: best RI observed across all methods/datasets: 2.87% (StacNAS on CIFAR100)

claim: The training protocol (Cutout, DropPath, AutoAugment, extended epochs, more channels) contributes a larger accuracy swing than any observed search-algorithm gain, meaning most reported NAS state-of-the-art gains come from engineering the evaluation pipeline, not from the search strategy.
stance_target: search-space and training-protocol confounds dominate reported NAS gains, undermining claims about search-algorithm quality
scope_conditions: DARTS CIFAR10 search space, 10 training-protocol variants tested
quoted_support: a large difference of over 3 percentage points (p.p.) exists between the simplest and the most advanced training protocols. Indeed, this is much higher than any improvement over random sampling observed in the previous section: for example, on CIFAR10, the best improvement observed was 0.69 p.p.
numbers: 98.15% best accuracy with best protocol on random architecture, 0.25pp below SOTA

claim: 214 architectures randomly sampled from the DARTS CIFAR10 search space all cluster within roughly one accuracy point of each other, demonstrating the search space itself is narrow/well-engineered such that nearly any sampled architecture performs well.
stance_target: narrow search spaces make it structurally hard for any search algorithm to beat random sampling by a large margin
scope_conditions: DARTS search space, CIFAR10, 214 fully-trained randomly sampled architectures
quoted_support: architectures sampled from this search space all perform similarly, with a mean of 97.03 +/- 0.23. The worst architecture we found had an accuracy of 96.18, while the best achieved 97.56.

claim: Changing only the random seed (same architecture, same training protocol) produces a Kendall-tau rank correlation of just 0.48 between two independent training runs, showing that single-seed architecture rankings in NAS are statistically unreliable.
stance_target: single-run, single-seed comparisons in NAS are not statistically trustworthy and multiple seeds are required
scope_conditions: DARTS search space, 32 randomly sampled architectures, two random seeds (A and B)
quoted_support: Ranking is heavily influenced, as the Kendall tau correlation between the two sets of training is 0.48. On average, the test accuracy changes by 0.13% +/- 0.08 (max change is 0.39%), which is substantial considering the small gap between random architectures and NAS methods.

claim: Changing the number of cells (8 vs 20) between search and final evaluation produces a Kendall-tau rank correlation of only 0.54, with individual architectures shifting up to 18 of 32 ranking positions -- the 'depth-gap' phenomenon.
stance_target: architecture rankings measured during search do not reliably transfer to the deployed/evaluated configuration
scope_conditions: DARTS search space, 32 randomly sampled architectures, 8-cell vs 20-cell configurations
quoted_support: The correlation between the two different depths is not very strong as measured by Kendall Tau (0.54), with architectures shifting up and down the rankings by up to 18 positions (out of 32).

claim: Restricting the available operation set to an intentionally impoverished, parameter-inefficient set of convolutions/pooling shifts mean architecture accuracy by only 0.18 accuracy points relative to the standard DARTS operation set, showing hand-designed macro-structure (cell wiring) matters far more than which micro-level operations are searched.
stance_target: the searched component of NAS (choice of operations) contributes little relative to the human-designed macro-structure, bounding how much credit any search algorithm -- LLM-based or otherwise -- can claim for good final accuracy
scope_conditions: DARTS-style cell search space on CIFAR10, comparison of standard 8-operation set vs a deliberately worse 6-operation set
quoted_support: The two distributions are only shifted by 0.18 accuracy points. Given the minor difference in performance, the specific operations are not a key ingredient in the success of this search space.
numbers: 56 architectures in modified space vs 214 in standard space

claim: Recommended NAS evaluation protocol includes: report accuracy with and without evaluation-protocol tricks, quantify search-space variability via random sampling with mean/std, and use NAS-Bench-101 to isolate search-strategy quality from search-space and training-protocol confounds.
stance_target: what constitutes an adequate NAS evaluation protocol
quoted_support: NAS-Bench-101 (Ying et al. 2019), a dataset mapping architectures to their accuracy, can be extremely useful, as it allows the quality of search strategies to be assessed in isolation from other NAS components (e.g. search space, training protocol) in a quick and reproducible fashion.
